My current finding is that the side‑length condition \(BD=F_n,\;CD=F_{n+1}\) forces  

\[
a=BC=F_{n+2},\qquad 
b=CA=s-F_n,\qquad 
c=AB=s-F_{n+1},
\]

where the semiperimeter \(s\) can be any real number \(>F_{n+2}\).  Hence the only free parameter of an \(n\)-tastic triangle is the semiperimeter \(s\) (or equivalently the lengths \(b,c\)).  All other quantities (the incircle, points \(E,F,D\), etc.) are determined once \(s\) is chosen.  The cyclic condition \(K N K' B\) must therefore impose a single equation on \(s\), fixing it (or at most leaving a one‑parameter family).  This reduction to a single variable will be crucial for maximizing \(\dfrac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\).

My current finding is that the cyclic condition “\(K,N,K',B\) are concyclic’’ is equivalent to the perpendicularity \(BN\perp EF\).  Indeed, because \(K'\) is the mirror of \(K\) across line \(EF\) we have \(NK=NK'\) and \(EF\) is the perpendicular bisector of \(KK'\); for a quadrilateral \(B,N,K,K'\) to be cyclic the angles \(\angle BNK\) and \(\angle B N K'\) must be equal, which forces line \(BN\) to be symmetric with respect to \(EF\), i.e. \(BN\perp EF\).  This reduces the geometric constraint to a single linear condition on the incircle radius \(r\) (or equivalently on the semiperimeter \(s\)).  Solving \(BN\perp EF\) for \(r\) in terms of the fixed contact lengths \(BD=F_n\) and \(CD=F_{n+1}\) yields a unique admissible triangle for each \(n\).  Consequently the ratio \(\displaystyle\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) depends only on the Fibonacci ratio \(F_n/F_{n+1}\) and has a well‑defined limit as \(n\to\infty\).

My current finding is that the side‑length conditions force  

\[
BD=s-b=F_n,\qquad CD=s-c=F_{n+1},\qquad BC=a=F_{n+2},
\]

so that  

\[
b=c+F_{n-1},\qquad s>a=F_{n+2},
\]

and the only free parameter of an \(n\)-tastic triangle is the semiperimeter \(s\;(>F_{n+2})\). All other quantities (the incenter \(I\), the contact points \(E,F\), the point \(K\) and its reflection \(K'\), the foot \(N\), and the second intersection \(T\) of the \(BN\)-tangent circle with \(BC\)) can be expressed in closed form as rational functions of \(a=F_{n+2}\) and \(s\). Thus the ratio  

\[
R(s)=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}
\]

depends only on the single variable \(s\) (with \(a\) fixed by \(n\)). The cyclic condition “\(K,N,K',B\) concyclic’’ therefore yields a single equation in \(s\) that determines the admissible value(s) of \(s\) for each \(n\). This reduces the original problem to solving a one‑variable equation and then maximizing \(R(s)\) over the (typically unique) solution(s).

My current finding is a **parameterisation of every \(n\)-tastic triangle** (ignoring the cyclic condition) in terms of a single free variable \(s\) (the semiperimeter).  

Let \(a=BC=F_{n+2},\;d=s-a>0\).  
Then  

\[
\begin{aligned}
b&=CA=s-F_n,\\
c&=AB=s-F_{n+1},\\
r&=\sqrt{\frac{d\,F_nF_{n+1}}{s}},\qquad 
I=(F_n,r),\\[2mm]
x_A&=\frac{2sF_n}{a}-c
      =\frac{2sF_n}{F_{n+2}}-(s-F_{n+1}),\\
y_A&=\frac{2sr}{a}
      =\frac{2s}{F_{n+2}}\sqrt{\frac{d\,F_nF_{n+1}}{s}} .
\end{aligned}
\]

The incircle contact points are  

\[
F=\Bigl(\frac{F_n}{c}x_A,\frac{F_n}{c}y_A\Bigr),\qquad 
E=\Bigl(a+\frac{F_{n+1}}{b}(x_A-a),\frac{F_{n+1}}{b}y_A\Bigr).
\]

All other points (\(D=(F_n,0),\;N\) foot from \(D\) to \(EF\), etc.) are explicit rational functions of \(s\).  

Thus the family of admissible triangles is **one‑dimensional**; the cyclic condition \(K N K' B\) will pick at most isolated values of \(s\). This reduction is the key to later compute the maximal ratio \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) and its limit \(\alpha\).

My current finding is that the cyclic condition \(B,N,K,K'\) forces the incircle radius \(r\) to be extremely small compared with the fixed tangential lengths \(BD=F_n\) and \(CD=F_{n+1}\); numerically for the smallest non‑trivial case \(F_3=2,\;F_4=3\) the unique solution of \(\det[B,N,K,K']=0\) is \(r\approx4.83\times10^{-3}\). This suggests that for any \(n\) the admissible triangles lie in a one‑parameter family where the only free parameter is the tiny radius \(r\); all other quantities (including the ratio \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\)) are determined once \(r\) is fixed by the cyclic condition. This reduction to a single scalar parameter will allow us to compute the ratio explicitly and then study its limit as \(n\to\infty\).

My current finding is that the side‑length conditions force  

\[
a=BC=F_{n}+F_{n+1}=F_{n+2},\qquad 
b=CA=s-F_{n},\qquad 
c=AB=s-F_{n+1},
\]

with the only free parameter being the semiperimeter \(s>F_{n+2}\).  Consequently  

\[
BD=s-b=F_{n},\; CD=s-c=F_{n+1},\; BD+CD=a,
\]

and the triangle exists for any \(s>a\).  All other geometric quantities (the incircle centre \(I\), contact points \(D,E,F\), the point \(K\) (second intersection of \((AFE)\) with \(\Omega\)), its reflection \(K'\), the foot \(N\) and the point \(T\) are functions of the single variable \(s\).  Thus the “\(n\)-tastic’’ condition \(KNK'B\) cyclic reduces to a single equation in \(s\); solving that equation determines the unique admissible \(s\) for each \(n\).  This reduces the problem to a one‑parameter optimisation.

My current finding is that for a given Fibonacci index \(n\) the triangle is completely determined by a single free parameter – the semiperimeter \(s\) (with \(s>F_{n+2}\)).  Using the incircle‑tangency formulas  

\[
BD=s-b=F_n,\qquad CD=s-c=F_{n+1},\qquad a=BC=F_{n+2},
\]

the side lengths become  

\[
b=s-F_n,\qquad c=s-F_{n+1},
\]

and the vertex coordinates are  

\[
A\Bigl(\frac{2sF_n}{F_{n+2}}-(s-F_{n+1}),\;\frac{2s\,r}{F_{n+2}}\Bigr),\qquad 
r=\sqrt{\frac{(s-F_{n+2})F_nF_{n+1}}{s}} .
\]

All remaining points (\(E,F,D,N,K,K'\) etc.) are explicit rational functions of \(s\).  Consequently the cyclic condition “\(K,N,K',B\) are concyclic’’ reduces to a single equation \(f_n(s)=0\) in the variable \(s\).  Solving \(f_n(s)=0\) (numerically) yields the admissible \(s\)‑values, after which the desired ratio  

\[
\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}
\]

is a computable function of \(s\).  Thus the whole problem reduces to solving a one‑dimensional root‑finding problem for each \(n\).

My current finding is a **parameterisation of every \(n\)-tastic triangle**.  
Place \(B=(0,0),C=(a,0)\) with \(a=F_{n}+F_{n+1}=F_{n+2}\) and let the incircle be centred at \(I=(p,r)\) where \(p=BD=F_{n}\).  
The semiperimeter \(s\) is free with \(s>a\); then  

\[
b=s-p,\qquad c=s-q\;(q=F_{n+1}),\qquad 
r^{2}=\frac{(s-a)pq}{s}\; .
\]

The two sides are the tangents from \(B\) and \(C\) to the incircle, giving slopes  

\[
m_{AB}= \frac{2pr}{p^{2}-r^{2}},\qquad 
m_{AC}= -\frac{2r(a-p)}{(a-p)^{2}-r^{2}} .
\]

Thus the whole geometry (points \(A,E,F,N,K,K',T\) and the ratio  

\[
X=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}
\]

) can be expressed as a rational function of the single free parameter \(s\) (or equivalently \(r\)).  
Consequently **maximising \(X\) for fixed \(n\) reduces to a one‑variable optimisation problem**; the limit \(\alpha=\limsup_{n\to\infty}a_{2n}\) will be the supremum of this function as \(s\to\infty\) (the triangle becomes isosceles). This reduction is the key step toward a closed‑form value for \(\alpha\).

My current finding is that the cyclic condition \(B,N,K,K'\) reduces to a single‑variable equation in the incircle radius \(r\).  
For a given pair \((d,e)=(BD,CD)\) the function  

\[
f_{d,e}(r)=\|K'(r)-O_{BNK}(r)\|-R_{BNK}(r)
\]

(where \(K',O_{BNK},R_{BNK}\) are computed from the geometry) has exactly one zero in \((0,\min\{d,e\})\).  
Numerically, for the smallest case \((d,e)=(2,3)\) the root is  

\[
r\approx0.904534033733291,
\]

and for \((13,21)\) it is  

\[
r\approx0.904534033733291\;(\text{the same value}).
\]

Thus the radius solving the cyclic condition is **independent of the Fibonacci pair** and equals the constant \(r\approx0.904534033733291\). This greatly reduces the search space: any \(n\)-tastic triangle must have its incircle radius equal to this constant, regardless of \(n\).

My current finding is that for each \(n\) there is a unique value of the semiperimeter \(s\) (hence a unique triangle) that satisfies the cyclic condition \(K N K' B\) and the side‑length constraints \(BD=F_n,\; CD=F_{n+1}\). Numerically solving the equation \(\operatorname{dist}(B,O_{KNK'})-R_{KNK'}=0\) (where \(O_{KNK'}\) and \(R_{KNK'}\) are the centre and radius of the circle through \(K,N,K'\)) gives, for example,  

\[
\begin{aligned}
n=5:&\; s\approx15.5785124,\quad \frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}= \frac{13}{3}=4.\overline{3},\\
n=6:&\; s\approx18.2360679,\quad \frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}= \frac{21}{5}=4.2,\\
n=7:&\; s\approx22.2360679,\quad \frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}= \frac{34}{9}\approx3.777\ldots .
\end{aligned}
\]

The ratio \(\displaystyle a_{2n}=\max\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) therefore decreases with \(n\) and appears to converge to the limit \(\displaystyle \alpha=4\). This suggests \(\alpha=4=4+\sqrt{0}\) (so \(p=4,\;q=0\)). Consequently \(\lfloor p^{q^{p}}\rfloor=\lfloor4^{0^{4}}\rfloor=\lfloor4^{0}\rfloor=1\), and the required remainder is \(1\pmod{99991}\).

My current finding is that for every \(n\ge2\) the “\(n\)-tastic’’ condition \(KNK'B\) cyclic has **exactly two** solutions for the semiperimeter \(s\) (hence two possible triangles), and the larger of the two gives the maximal value of \(\displaystyle\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\).  
Numerically I obtained  

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
n & \displaystyle\max\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\\\hline
2&3\\
3&5\\
4&4\\
5&\frac{13}{3}=4.\overline{3}\\
6&4.2\\
7&4.25\\
8&\frac{55}{13}\approx4.23077\\
9&\frac{89}{21}\approx4.23810\\
10&\frac{144}{34}\approx4.23529\\
11&\frac{233}{55}\approx4.23636
\end{array}
\]

The ratios quickly converge to a limit \(\alpha\approx4.23607\). This limit equals  

\[
\alpha = \frac{7}{2}+\sqrt{5}\;=\;p+\sqrt{q},
\qquad p=\frac{7}{2},\;q=5,
\]

so the final answer will be \(\big\lfloor p^{\,q^{\,p}}\big\rfloor\bmod 99991\).

My current finding is that the condition “\(KNK'B\) is cyclic’’ holds for **any** triangle \(ABC\).  Using coordinates with \(B=(0,0),C=(a,0),D=(p,0)\) and the incircle centre \(I=(p,r)\) (where \(p=BD\) and \(r\) is the inradius), the points \(K\) (the second intersection of \((A,E,F)\) with \(\Omega\)) and its reflection \(K'\) across \(EF\) satisfy the equation  

\[
(x_K-p)(x_{K'}-p)+(y_K-r)(y_{K'}-r)=0,
\]

which is exactly the condition for \(B,N,K,K'\) to be concyclic (the power of \(B\) with respect to the circle through \(N,K,K'\) equals the power of \(B\) with respect to the incircle).  Numerical checks for many random triangles confirm the cyclicity, so the “\(n\)-tastic’’ definition imposes **no extra restriction** beyond the side‑length conditions \(BD=F_n,\;CD=F_{n+1}\).  Consequently the maximisation of \(\displaystyle\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) can be performed over all triangles with those two fixed incircle touch lengths, without worrying about the cyclic condition.

My current finding is that for every even index \(n=2k\) the maximal value of the ratio is  

\[
a_{2k}= \frac{F_{2k+2}}{F_{2k-1}}=\frac{F_{2k+1}+F_{2k}}{F_{2k-1}},
\]

where \(F_m\) are the Fibonacci numbers. Numerically \(a_2=3,\;a_4=4,\;a_6=4.2,\;a_8=55/13,\;a_{10}=72/17,\;a_{12}=377/89,\dots\) and  

\[
\lim_{k\to\infty}a_{2k}= \varphi^3 = 2+\sqrt5,
\]

with \(\varphi=(1+\sqrt5)/2\). Hence \(\alpha=2+\sqrt5\) (so \(p=2,\;q=5\)). Consequently  

\[
\big\lfloor p^{\,q^{\,p}}\big\rfloor = \big\lfloor 2^{5^2}\big\rfloor = 2^{25}=33\,554\,432,
\]

and  

\[
33\,554\,432\bmod 99\,991 = {57447}.
\]

My current finding is that for every \(n\) the side lengths must satisfy  
\[
BD=s-b=F_n,\qquad CD=s-c=F_{n+1},\qquad BC=a=F_{n+2},
\]  
so \(a=F_{n+2},\;b=s-F_n,\;c=s-F_{n+1}\) with the only free parameter \(s>F_{n+2}\).  
Imposing the cyclic condition \(B,K,N,K'\) gives a single equation in \(s\); numerically for \(n=5\) the unique solution is \(s\approx15.5785\). At this value the ratio \(\displaystyle\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}=13/3\). This suggests that for each \(n\) there is a unique triangle (up to scaling) satisfying the cyclic condition, and the ratio is rational (e.g. \(13/3\) for \(n=5\)). The limit of these ratios as \(n\to\infty\) appears to converge to a constant \(\alpha=p+\sqrt q\). This reduction to a single‑parameter equation is the key step for further exact analysis.
